Linney and Hecht are excellent and generous scene partners, and though Summer, 1976 has none of the explosive bells and whistles of some of its Broadway compadres, it has its own gentle, unassuming power.
In fact, if this accessible and often charming play won’t earn Mr. Auburn another Pulitzer, I can easily picture it enduring as a showcase for any number of gifted actresses.
Linney and Hecht’s confident, vulnerable-lite performances are the reasons to come, and the two stage veterans embrace the audience with their affable warmth and charm.
That said, it’s not quite enough to make Auburn’s play a Summer to remember.
And so was I happy for a time, to bask in the company of these two phenomenally persuasive and appealing actresses.

Summer, 1976 comes off as a literary exercise, an enacted short story about a series of situational connections with others that happen to most of us most of the time.
Under Daniel Sullivan’s sure-handed direction, they offer a marvelous masterclass in acting (on John Lee Beatty’s ingenious set).
It's a measure of the care with which Summer, 1976 has been written, produced, and performed that, days later, you may find yourself musing about Diana and Alice.
But, when the two women conversing are played by Laura Linney and Jessica Hecht, this is a tête-à-tête that is worth overhearing.
Mr. Auburn may not have written the next great American play, but what he and his talented collaborators have provided is definitely worth the 90 minutes it takes to engage with it.
It was a delight to experience the result of all of their work.
While brilliantly acted by Laura Linney and Jessica Hecht (both of them smartly costumed by Linda Cho), the 90-minute play ultimately feels like a stretched-out anecdote.
But at present, it feels like a star vehicle hastily slapped together, promising much and delivering little.
